title: 5 Best Modern Treasury Alternatives & Competitors in 2026
summary: Compare Modern Treasury alternatives for bank connectivity, programmable ledgers, reconciliation, multi-asset flows, and self-hosted deployment.
body_markdown:
Modern Treasury built its reputation on US bank connectivity, automating ACH, wires, and reconciliation for teams moving fiat between US bank accounts. That focus is a strength for US-only treasury operations, but it is a ceiling for teams whose money problem is bigger than a US payment-operations platform.


### Why teams consider Modern Treasury alternatives


Five triggers push teams to evaluate Modern Treasury alternatives, and most reach out after hitting two or three at once:


1


**Multi-country rollouts** run into Modern Treasury's US-heavy bank network, leaving teams to stitch non-US rails together outside the platform.


2


**Stablecoin and tokenized-asset flows** demand a general-purpose digital-asset model, not a stablecoin bolt-on grafted onto a fiat ledger.


3


**Data-residency requirements** under DORA, MiCA, or GDPR require deployment on the customer's own cloud in a specific region, and a hosted-only platform becomes a hard procurement blocker.


4


**Product logic that belongs inside the ledger** (complex fee splits, sub-account hierarchies, multi-party settlement, cross-currency conversions) forces engineering teams to reconstruct transaction semantics in application code when the managed ledger cannot express them natively.


5


**Closed-source procurement blockers** , such as security and procurement teams at regulated entities, often refuse a closed-source system of record, requiring source-level auditability and the option to fork.


The five best Modern Treasury alternatives in 2026 are Formance, TigerBeetle, Fragment, Stripe's ledger primitives, and building in-house, benchmarked against Modern Treasury.

### Formance is an open-source programmable core ledger for multi-asset money movement


Formance is an open-source, programmable core ledger platform that unifies fiat and digital assets with[regulatory-grade traceability](https://www.formance.com/blog/financial-operations/ensuring-ledger-integrity) . The ledger offers a real-time double-entry engine with bi-temporal history and append-only postings.


It also includes modules for Connectivity, Flows and Reconciliation.


Formance is a system of record and not a money movement platform. Formance does not hold or move funds itself. All money movement flows through connected payment providers (PSPs, banks, exchanges, or custodians).


The distinguishing primitive is[Numscript](https://www.formance.com/platform/numscript) , a purpose-built DSL for describing multi-party financial transactions. You write the transaction once, and Numscript handles the fee splits, sub-account movements, and currency conversions as a single atomic operation. Every leg commits together, or none commits at all, so the ledger never lands in a partial state.


A marketplace payout that splits a $100,000 customer payment across a merchant, a platform fee, and a tax-holding account looks like this in Numscript:


```text
send   [USD/2 10000000]   (
source   =   @world
destination   = {
80  %   to   @merchant:acme
15  %   to   @platform:fees
5  %   to   @tax:holding
}
)


```


The three destinations settle atomically. If any leg fails, none of the postings commit, so the ledger cannot end up in a partial state where the merchant is credited, but the tax holding is not.


[Formance's connectors directly counter Modern Treasury's US-centric rail depth](https://www.formance.com/blog/competitive/formance-vs-modern-treasury) and Fragment's zero-connector model. Pre-built connectors span eight categories (PSPs, cross-border, BaaS, direct-API banks, Open Banking, digital asset custody, crypto exchanges, and direct on-chain rails), covering vendors like Stripe, Wise, JP Morgan, Fireblocks, and Coinbase.


For providers outside the pre-built list, teams typically build a custom integration in 2 to 4 weeks using the open-source generic connector framework.


#### Formance wins on open source, deployment, compliance, and scale


•


**True open source:**[MIT-licensed](https://github.com/formancehq/ledger/blob/main/LICENSE) with source-level auditability, no vendor lock-in, and the option to fork the codebase to meet internal engineering standards.


•


**Deploys on your own infrastructure:** Three tiers available (Community Edition, Enterprise Self-Hosted, and Enterprise Private Cloud) covering AWS, GCP, and Azure, meeting DORA, GDPR, and country-specific banking data-residency requirements.


•


**Compliance certifications inherit downstream:** Customers deploying Formance as a sub-ledger reduce their own SOC 2 and ISO 27001 audit scope by inheriting certified controls from the platform.


•


**Proven at scale:** Liberis uses Formance to power embedded finance across[14 countries](https://www.formance.com/blog/customer-story/liberis) with zero reconciliation errors, handling bundled transactions and split mechanisms between multiple partners without adding headcount. As Liberis noted: "Formance enabled us to ship new lending products faster by providing a customizable foundation that let us reliably express the complexities of our flow of funds."


#### Formance struggles with operator UX, payment rails, and self-hosting cost


•


**Engineering-first product:** API-first integration with no drag-and-drop dashboard for finance operators.


•


**You bring the rails:** Not a payment-operations platform, so treasury workflows like wire approval may need a payment-ops layer above Formance.


•


**Self-hosting overhead:** Kubernetes deployment requires dedicated platform engineering resources.


### TigerBeetle is a high-throughput OLTP storage engine for financial transactions


TigerBeetle is a purpose-built OLTP database for financial transactions, written in Zig with a fixed schema tuned for accounting workloads. It is a storage engine and not a direct ledger platform.


Treating TigerBeetle as a drop-in replacement for Modern Treasury Ledgers or[Formance Ledger will fail](https://www.formance.com/blog/competitive/formance-vs-tigerbeetle) . Treated as a fast, correctness-focused backing store for a ledger you build on top of, TigerBeetle earns its place.


The engine is built for multi-object transactions under high contention. TigerBeetle co-locates the accounting logic with the storage and runs as a six-replica distributed system, reducing each transfer to a handful of in-memory operations. The result is what the docs call the "speed-of-light" path for financial state changes.


TigerBeetle is designed to run alongside a general-purpose database like Postgres. TigerBeetle handles accounts, transfers, and balance updates in the hot path. Postgres (or Formance, or your app database) stores everything else: metadata, user records, and business logic.


#### TigerBeetle's strengths in throughput, correctness, and disaster recovery


•


**Extreme throughput:** Designed to handle up to 1M transfers per second, per the vendor's stated target. It is real for utility billing, ad-network settlements, or per-second serverless billing.


•


**Correctness at the engine level:** Real-time balance limits (hard or dynamic) are guaranteed per-account, and debits can never exceed credits or vice versa.


•


**Strong disaster-recovery story:** Six-replica cluster using Viewstamped Replication with a flexible 3-of-6 write quorum. The cluster stays available through multiple node failures and is designed to halt rather than lose committed data if quorum can't be met


•


**Built-in two-phase transfers:** Pending amounts are authorized in phase one and posted or voided in phase two with timeouts managed by the database, 2PC across third-party systems natively.


•


**Apache 2.0 licensed:** with an active engineering culture and detailed public design docs.


#### TigerBeetle has trade-offs on connectors, tooling, and API maturity


•


**You build the ledger with limitations:** You get no connectors, no reconciliation product, no orchestration layer, no dashboard, and no compliance UI.


•


**The two-database problem is real:** Transfer initiation must not fetch metadata from your general-purpose database, or that database becomes the bottleneck. Careful control-plane design and denormalized integer IDs are required.


•


**No authentication layer:** Untrusted users or services should never interact with TigerBeetle directly, so you're wrapping it in your own service layer.


•


**Reconciliation against external providers is entirely on you:** No Stripe connector, no bank statement parser, and no drift detection out of the box.


•


**API and query maturity are still evolving:** Fine if you're comfortable riding a fast-moving open-source project. Risky if change management requires a mature tooling ecosystem.


### Fragment is a hosted ledger API for fast time-to-production


Fragment is a hosted ledger API positioned as the fastest path from "we need a ledger" to "the ledger is running." Fragment's differentiator is a visual ledger simulator ('Scenarios') that lets teams model a chart of accounts and simulate transaction flows interactively before writing code. Fragment's own materials claim teams can set up the full ledger infrastructure in under a week.


It is useful during evaluation and replacing a typical two-week proof of concept (PoC). A short evaluation build where a team validates whether a vendor's product actually works for their use case before committing to a full integration. Stripe backed Fragment's[$9 million seed](https://techcrunch.com/2024/07/22/digital-ledger-fragment-9m-banks-balance-sheets) in July 2024, and the same report places total funding at $10.8 million.


Fragment's product surface is a ledger DSL, SDKs in multiple languages, sandbox and production environments, and a hosted infrastructure model. Fragment is the shortest path to production for early-stage teams that need a real double-entry ledger without running infrastructure or waiting through a six-month platform build.


Fragment's limits show at integration boundaries. Fragment lacks Modern Treasury's provider connectivity and[Formance's multi-asset breadth](https://www.formance.com/blog/competitive/formance-vs-fragment) , and complex multi-rail orchestration lands in your application layer. Fragment's team, funding, and enterprise readiness are also earlier-stage than mature vendors.


#### Fragment's advantages for startups shipping a ledger this quarter


•


**Fastest time to a working ledger:** Visual simulator and interactive simulations in under 30 minutes.


•


**Developer-friendly ergonomics:** Ledger API, language SDKs, sandbox and production options, and well-documented onboarding.


•


**Strong fit for early-stage, cloud-comfortable startups:** Teams that want production readiness without building or self-hosting infrastructure.


•


**Backed by Stripe:** an investor signal for teams already in the Stripe ecosystem.


#### The gaps Fragment leaves for regulated and multi-rail teams


•


**Hosted only:** Data-residency or self-hosting requirements are effectively a blocker.


•


**No connectivity or orchestration layer:** You integrate PSPs, banks, and custodians yourself, and comparing internal balances against Stripe, Adyen, or a bank statement is application-layer work.


•


**Early-stage vendor risk:** Procurement at regulated entities should weigh long-term operating fit against Fragment's early-stage status.


### Stripe's ledger primitives are built-in record-keeping for Stripe-native stacks


Stripe's ledger primitives (balances, transactions, Connect account records, and Issuing authorizations) are tied to Stripe's payment products and live inside Stripe's platform. Stripe has extended this with Financial Accounts for Platforms (formerly Stripe Treasury), which adds FDIC pass-through insured accounts, direct ACH and wire transfers, multi-currency balances, and stablecoin-backed balances in 100+ countries.


But even with that expansion, Stripe's primitives remain a record-keeping layer for money that moves through Stripe's own network of bank and rail partnerships. They are not a general-purpose ledger.


The moment money moves through a rail or partner Stripe doesn't support natively (a direct bank relationship outside Stripe's partner network, a non-Stripe merchant of record, RTP or FedNow access Stripe doesn't offer, or a PSP) Stripe's primitives stop being sufficient as a system of record.


You now have "Stripe balances" and "not-Stripe balances," with no atomic ledger across both, and discovering the need for a unified ledger at that point is costly.


#### Where Stripe's ledger primitives deliver value for single-rail businesses


•


**Zero additional vendor cost:** Included with the Stripe products you're already using.


•


**Real-time and Stripe-authoritative:** Balances and transaction records are always in sync with Stripe's view of the world.


•


**Sufficient for Stripe-native stacks:** where every dollar moves through Stripe and you expect that to remain true.


#### The limits of Stripe's primitives once a second rail enters the picture


•


**Not a general-purpose ledger:** No modeling of non-Stripe balances, no multi-rail postings, no cross-provider reconciliation.


•


**No self-hosted or portable option:** Data stays in Stripe, and extraction for audit or migration is a separate exercise.


•


**No separate ledger product to certify:** Compliance posture is Stripe's platform posture.


•


**Rail lock-in:** Architectural pressure to keep money movement inside Stripe, even when a direct bank integration would be cheaper or faster.


### Building your own ledger means owning every layer indefinitely


[Building your own ledger](https://www.formance.com/blog/competitive/build-vs-buy-a-ledger-engineering) means owning every layer (concurrency, idempotency, multi-party transactions, bi-temporal history, reconciliation against external providers, and regulatory-grade traceability) as an ongoing engineering commitment rather than a one-time build. Any competent team can build a ledger that works in a demo. Keeping the ledger working through years of scaling events, new rails, and audit cycles is the harder problem.


The honest question isn't "can we build a ledger?" It's "is the ledger the product we sell?" If the ledger is the product, build it. If not, every engineer-week spent on ledger internals is one not spent on the product customers pay for.


Audit-readiness is a separate milestone from "works in production." SOC 2 controls, evidence collection, immutability proofs, and a documented reconciliation process are what turn a working ledger into an auditable one.


#### Why teams choose to build a ledger from scratch


•


**Total design control:** You define every data model choice, posting semantic, and API contract to match your exact business logic.


•


**No vendor licensing, no lock-in, no roadmap dependency:** You own the code, the release cadence, and every feature decision, with no third-party contract to renegotiate.


•


**Optimized for your exact workload:** A custom build is the right answer when no vendor addresses your requirement, whether that's an unusual asset class, a novel transaction shape, or a specific latency target.


#### The hidden costs of building and maintaining a ledger in-house


•


**Audit-readiness and compliance certifications are your project to run:** "Works in production" does not equal "passes SOC 2 and a Big 4 financial audit." SOC 2 Type II, ISO 27001, DORA, and MiCA are all your audit to pass without a vendor's certifications to inherit from.


•


**Every scaling event reopens the ledger:** New rail, new geography, new asset class, new regulator. Each one is a ledger-schema conversation and a migration.


•


**Ongoing engineer drag:** One or two senior engineers indefinitely, versus what those engineers would otherwise ship.


### Which Modern Treasury alternative fits your needs


Choose the alternative that matches where your money problem lives: in a programmable multi-asset core (Formance), in a high-throughput engine (TigerBeetle), in a fast-start hosted ledger (Fragment), inside Stripe (Stripe primitives), or in a custom build.


•


**Formance** : Multi-rail fintech or regulated entity building product logic inside the ledger: fee splits, sub-account hierarchies, flows across fiat and digital assets, self-hosted deployment for data sovereignty, and DORA/MiCA/GENIUS compliance work already in progress. Deploys beside a payment-operations layer when you need both.


•


**TigerBeetle:** The ledger engine is itself your product, or your workload genuinely requires more than 100K TPS with strong contention. Budget for the two-database architecture and the application code required to turn a storage engine into a ledger product.


•


**Fragment:** Early-stage, cloud-comfortable, wants a working ledger this quarter. Stress-test the hosted deployment against data-residency requirements first.


•


**Stripe's ledger primitives:** Entirely Stripe-native, expected to remain so, no non-Stripe balances or rails on the roadmap.


•


**Build in-house:** Only if the ledger is the product you sell, or you have a genuinely unusual requirement no vendor addresses.
